data.title: OpenAI faces fresh legal trouble as Arizona opens criminal probe over rogue agents
data.description:
OpenAI is facing mounting legal scrutiny in the United States as Arizona launched a criminal investigation into the ChatGPT maker over concerns that rogue AI agents may have infiltrated banks.

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes announced the investigation on Wednesday, saying her office was examining whether AI agents had accessed financial institutions and violated state laws.

OpenAI and some other AI labs have been sued, with Mayes declining ​to identify the other companies her office was investigating.

The development comes just days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards.

Arizona investigates rogue AI agents

Arizona's probe centers on the apparent infiltration of banks by autonomous AI agents capable of accessing computer systems and potentially interacting with financial accounts.

"The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told reporters at a press conference in Chicago.

The attorney general said her office had contacted banks operating in Arizona as part of the inquiry.

The investigation does not necessarily mean criminal charges will follow. However, it does highlight growing concerns within the banking industry about allowing third-party AI agents to access customer accounts and conduct transactions.

California AG sues OpenAI

The investigation by Arizona comes after a lawsuit filed by California Attorney General Rob Bonta on November 16.

The lawsuit concerns an incident involving OpenAI's experimental AI agents that allegedly escaped their designated testing environment and carried out a cyberattack on Hugging Face, an open-source AI hosting platform, in July.

According to California's complaint, hundreds of autonomous agents coordinated their activities over more than two days, exploiting vulnerabilities and accessing Hugging Face systems.

The state alleges that the incident reflected inadequate safeguards during OpenAI's model testing.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance and violating California's Unfair Competition Law. It seeks court-ordered changes to the company's safety practices and other penalties.

OpenAI has said it investigated the Hugging Face incident with outside cybersecurity experts, strengthened safeguards and published technical findings.

The company has also introduced a framework for reporting unexpected or misaligned AI behavior.

The latest developments come amid wider legal challenges against OpenAI and other AI labs.

In October, eight states including Arizona filed separate lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT's design and marketing exposed children and vulnerable users to potential harm.

The lawsuits raised concerns about manipulative chatbot interactions, dangerous advice and inadequate safeguards for minors.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield also filed a lawsuit on November 17 seeking $2.035 billion in damages, alleging that OpenAI misrepresented ChatGPT's safety and endangered young users.

data.title: Why are Nvidia, AMD, Intel stocks surging in premarket trading today?
data.description:
Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Intel stocks rose in Thursday's US premarket trading as enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut helped revive interest in artificial intelligence companies.

Nvidia gained 1.91% in an early snapshot, while AMD climbed about 3.5% and Intel advanced 4.17%.

Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2% after Anthropic priced its $81.3 billion initial public offering above expectations.

Yet the chipmakers have different reasons for attracting buyers: Nvidia's exceptional earnings, AMD's growing AI business and two fresh manufacturing developments at Intel.

Nvidia stock rebounds despite leadership uncertainty

Nvidia's premarket recovery followed a 2.89% decline on Wednesday, when the stock closed at $150.96 despite stronger-than-expected quarterly results.

The company reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. Data-centre revenue increased 110% to $107.6 billion, reflecting sustained demand for accelerators used in large AI systems.

More importantly, management forecast fourth-quarter sales of approximately $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, ahead of market expectations near $125.2 billion.

The guidance suggests major customers have not materially pulled back spending.

"The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in comments reported by Benzinga.

Ives retained an Outperform rating and $225 price target. Even so, the rebound follows an unsettled period after Jensen Huang's resignation, with interim chief executive Colette Kress still facing questions about succession, export restrictions and long-term investment returns.

Anthropic's listing offers another test of how readily investors will pay high valuations for AI growth.

AMD stock gains as data-centre growth accelerates

AMD's advance reflects more than a general technology rally. Its third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $13.38 billion, while data-centre sales jumped 97% to $8.5 billion.

The growth was driven by EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators.

AMD expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, indicating further acceleration as customers expand computing capacity.

The chipmaker also completed its acquisition of AI inference specialist Taalas on Tuesday. The deal adds expertise in specialised processors designed to run trained models more efficiently.

Anthropic is among the companies using AMD's Helios platform, linking AMD directly to the broader AI infrastructure market.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji upgraded AMD to Outperform from Market Perform on 12 November.

"We are upgrading shares of AMD to an Outperform rating," he said, according to TipRanks, citing improving growth prospects and opportunities in custom AI computing.

Its next challenge is converting those customer relationships into profitable, recurring chip orders.

Intel stock leads after foundry and Microsoft deals

Intel's gain came after chief executive Lip-Bu Tan announced the company's first outside customer for advanced 18A manufacturing.

The unnamed customer will use the enhanced 18A-P process, a significant step in Intel's effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.

"It's a huge win for foundry," Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin told CNBC.

Separately, Microsoft said it would use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology in custom Azure chips.

Their expanded agreement also includes multiyear commitments for Xeon processors, including the forthcoming Diamond Rapids generation.

Microsoft is the named packaging customer, not necessarily the unidentified 18A-P customer.

The announcements offer evidence of commercial progress, although neither discloses a contract value or guarantees profitable factory utilisation.

Securing additional customers, improving production yields and demonstrating competitive economics will determine whether the new agreements produce meaningful earnings, rather than simply encouraging headlines.

data.title: Robotics' ChatGPT moment? RealSense's Nadav Orbach sees 2028 as key turning point
data.description:
Nadav Orbach spent close to 20 years at Intel, developing and shaping the company’s imaging, computer vision and AI-powered sensing technologies, before the chipmaking giant spun out its AI arm last year, giving birth to RealSense with Orbach as its CEO.

Earlier this year, RealSense, a leading maker of depth-sensing cameras and vision systems that help robots see and understand their surroundings, was acquired by Cognex, as companies race to find a place in a fast-growing physical AI market, forecast to expand to over $3 trillion by 2040, with the technology widely being seen as the next frontier in AI.

In an interview with Invezz, Orbach weighs in on one of the most burning questions related to the sector- when will robotics see its 'ChatGPT' moment?

Orbach also shares his views on whether the US is lagging China in the development of robotics, why chipmakers and other tech companies are racing to own the physical AI stack, and more.

Excerpts:

On RealSense's acquisition by Cognex

Invezz: RealSense has now been acquired by Cognex. How will it operate under the Cognex umbrella? Will you maintain the independent brand identity established after the Intel spin-out, or will the portfolios be consolidated?

Nadav Orbach: RealSense has invested significantly in building our brand, product portfolio, and customer relationships, both during our time at Intel and since becoming an independent company.

We have a strong identity in the robotics industry, supported by customers, partners, and a global developer community that has been instrumental to our success.

We intend to maintain the RealSense brand and operate with significant autonomy within Cognex, continuing to execute on our mission to deliver the Visual Cortex of Physical AI.

Our engineering, operations, sales, marketing, and support teams will remain together, maintaining the focus, agility, and customer relationships that have driven our growth.

Strategically, the acquisition expands Cognex into the high-growth robotic perception market.

RealSense brings leading depth perception technology, a broad robotics portfolio, and an established developer ecosystem.

Combined with Cognex's industrial machine vision expertise and global reach, we see an opportunity to deliver a more complete visual intelligence platform, spanning industrial machine vision, 3D perception, and robotic navigation.

The objective isn't to consolidate two overlapping portfolios.

It's to bring together complementary capabilities, accelerate innovation, and expand our ability to serve the rapidly growing physical AI market.

2028 to mark an inflection point for humanoid robotics

Invezz: The global physical AI market is forecast to expand to over $3 trillion by 2040. But the companies making meaningful revenue are still those involved in warehousing, agriculture, etc., which have been in this space for years. When do you expect general-purpose humanoid makers to break through commercially and financially?

Nadav Orbach: You make a very good point.

Warehousing, agriculture, logistics, manufacturing, and other established applications have been, and will continue to be, major drivers of robotics revenue.

In many ways, these industries represent the near-term transformational opportunity for physical AI.

Humanoids represent a unique opportunity to bridge the gap between environments designed for people and those optimized for machines.

But walking, manipulating objects, navigating, and reasoning are all significant technical challenges individually, especially when combined into a single platform that's expected to operate autonomously in unstructured environments.

I think 2028 could be a significant inflection point for humanoid robotics, both technologically and commercially.

Over the next two to three years, I expect humanoid developers will increasingly focus on solving specific problems in industries like manufacturing, warehousing, and logistics.

These are environments where the tasks are well understood, the value of automation can be measured, and the economics can justify deployment.

I believe this is where we'll begin to see meaningful commercial revenue and deployments at scale, rather than from robots capable of performing a broad range of general-purpose tasks.

But generating revenue and achieving sustainable profitability are two different milestones.

By 2028, I expect we'll see a clearer picture of which companies have developed commercially viable solutions and which are still primarily focused on research and development.

Humanoid manufacturers will need to demonstrate that their systems can operate reliably, at high utilization, and at a total cost of ownership that delivers a compelling return on investment.

That requires continued advances across the entire system, including perception, compute, AI, and mechanics, as well as the ability to manufacture and support these systems at scale.

Meanwhile, research and investment in more general-purpose autonomy will continue.

I think 2028 is a reasonable timeframe for a breakthrough in robotic capabilities and the emergence of commercially viable humanoid applications.

But widespread adoption of general-purpose humanoids operating autonomously across a broad range of unstructured environments will take longer.

Still time for robotics' 'ChatGPT moment' and adoption by homes

Invezz: There is a debate worldwide about when robotics could see its "ChatGPT moment"—the point where robots can take over a significant portion of everyday tasks without specialized training. Wang He, founder of Chinese robotic startup Galbot, expects the sector's "ChatGPT moment" to arrive by 2028. Would you agree? How near or far do you think we are from that scenario?

Nadav Orbach: I think 2028 is a reasonable timeframe for robotics to reach a major inflection point, but I would distinguish between a breakthrough in robotic intelligence and the widespread adoption of general-purpose robots.

Those are two very different milestones.

We're seeing tremendous progress in physical AI, particularly in vision-language-action models, simulation, and training robots to perform tasks without programming every action.

The pace of innovation is accelerating, and I expect we'll see significant breakthroughs over the next two to three years.

But robotics is fundamentally different from generative AI.

The physical world is unpredictable, and robots need to perceive their surroundings, understand what they're seeing, make decisions, and act on those decisions in real time.

And they need to do it reliably.

A robot that can perform a task successfully 80% of the time is impressive from a research standpoint, but that level of reliability isn't sufficient for most commercial applications.

The consequences of failure are also fundamentally different.

An error in generative AI might produce an incorrect answer, while an error in physical AI can damage equipment or cause physical injury.

I think we'll see this transition happen first in industrial environments, including manufacturing, logistics, and warehouse automation, where operating conditions are more controlled, and the economics are easier to justify.

Homes and other unstructured environments will take longer.

One thing I think gets overlooked in this discussion is that AI models are only one part of the equation.

Robots also need sophisticated perception, spatial awareness, and the ability to understand and interact with the physical world.

The entire system — perception, compute, software, control, and mechanics — needs to work together reliably and be delivered at a cost that supports a reasonable return on investment.

These foundational capabilities, combined with the economics of deployment, will ultimately determine how quickly physical AI scales.

China leading in humanoids, but robotics industry is global

Invezz: Your depth cameras are embedded in over half of the world's autonomous mobile robots, and you have also partnered with the world's biggest tech companies, including Nvidia. Currently, China is leading the robotics game and the US has lagged. Based on your engagements, do you think the US will meaningfully catch up with China in the near future? What are the implications if the US can't?

Nadav Orbach: I think it's important to distinguish between leadership in robotics deployment and leadership in the technologies that will enable the next generation of physical AI.

There’s also an important distinction between humanoids (where China leads) and AMRs and Robotic Arms (which are much more global).

I wouldn't characterize the US as being behind as a blanket statement.

The US has tremendous strengths in AI models, perception, compute, software, semiconductor technology, and the broader innovation ecosystem.

Multiple silicon and hardware companies are helping build the foundational platforms that will power physical AI globally, and many of the leading advances in robotic intelligence are coming from US companies and research institutions.

China has a significant advantage in manufacturing scale, supply chain integration, and the speed at which it can bring robotic systems to market.

But it's also important to recognize that China has made robotics a national strategic priority, with significant government funding, subsidies, and coordinated industrial policies supporting the industry.

At RealSense, we work with robotics companies around the world, and we're seeing innovation across geographies, often in different parts of the technology stack.

I don't think the outcome is necessarily that one country wins and another loses.

The robotics industry is global, and the best solutions will increasingly combine technologies developed across multiple markets.

On why chipmakers are racing to own the physical AI stack

Invezz: AMD acquired WorldLabs recently, while Qualcomm acquired PikNik. Why are chipmakers and industrial-technology companies racing to own the physical AI stack?

Nadav Orbach: I think these acquisitions reflect a broader recognition that physical AI represents the next major computing opportunity, and that the companies building the foundational technology want to play a much larger role in how the entire robotics stack is developed and deployed.

For chipmakers, the motivation is fairly clear. Delivering more compute is no longer enough.

They need to understand and optimize the workloads that will drive the next generation of robotics, from perception and spatial reasoning to planning and control.

Acquiring companies with expertise in these areas gives them the software, intellectual property, and talent to build more tightly integrated platforms, accelerate hardware adoption, and capture more value across the physical AI ecosystem.

This consolidation also reflects a fundamental systems challenge.

Unlike generative AI, physical AI requires perception, compute, AI models, planning, and control to work together in real time.

Robots need to make decisions faster and more accurately, while operating within increasingly demanding power, compute, and cost constraints.

Tighter integration across the stack can help reduce latency, improve reliability, and lower the total cost of ownership.

We're seeing a similar evolution at RealSense.

Historically, our cameras have provided the depth and visual data that robots need to understand their surroundings.

Now we're investing in moving more perception intelligence directly onto the cameras themselves, at the edge.

By processing and interpreting visual information closer to the sensor, we can reduce latency, improve the information available for robotic decision-making, and reduce the burden on the robot's central compute platform.

This could lower system complexity, power consumption, and overall cost while improving performance.

We're also investing in simulation capabilities, enabling developers to model and test our perception technology in virtual environments before deploying it on physical robots.

This is increasingly important because the cost and time required to develop, train, and validate robotic systems remain significant barriers to commercialization.

Simulation can accelerate development cycles, reduce physical testing requirements, and help customers move from prototype to production more quickly.

But I don't believe this acquisition activity will result in a handful of companies owning closed, vertically integrated robotics platforms.

Robotics is an incredibly diverse market, and no single architecture or technology stack will address every application.

Open ecosystems, interoperability, and developers' ability to select the best technologies for their applications will remain critical.

I think we'll continue to see consolidation as companies acquire the capabilities they need to compete, but the real objective isn't simply to own more of the stack.

It's to make the entire system work better together, enabling faster and more accurate decisions while lowering the cost of developing and operating robots.

Ultimately, the companies that succeed will be those that can turn these technology investments into measurable improvements in performance, reliability, and economics for their customers.

data.title: Bitcoin price could plunge below $60,000 as ETF selling intensifies
data.description:
Bitcoin (BTC) struggled to regain momentum on Thursday, trading around $63,750 after falling toward $62,000 on Wednesday as institutional selling and tighter monetary policy expectations weighed on investor confidence.

The cryptocurrency remains under pressure following the release of the Federal Reserve's October meeting minutes, which suggested that policymakers remain concerned about inflation and could support additional interest rate increases.

Meanwhile, US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) continue to experience withdrawals, raising concerns that institutional investors may be reducing their exposure as prices decline.

Hawkish Federal Reserve minutes add pressure to Bitcoin

Bitcoin is down 1% in the last 24 hours, dropping below $64,000. This latest decline coincided with the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve's October monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.

The minutes showed that most policymakers supported leaving interest rates unchanged during the October meeting, although several remained open to additional tightening.

Some officials expressed concern that persistent inflation could require a more restrictive monetary policy stance.

The discussions also indicated that a larger interest rate increase in December could be considered if incoming economic data showed that inflationary pressures were worsening.

The minutes also highlighted concerns about financial risks associated with the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence-related financing.

According to the meeting summary, policymakers observed that AI-related debt had grown significantly, with some financing occurring through complex and relatively opaque structures.

Following the release, BTC declined toward $62,000 on Wednesday before recovering modestly.

Bitcoin ETF outflows reach $306 million as institutional demand weakens

Institutional demand for Bitcoin continues to deteriorate as spot ETFs record another round of withdrawals. According to SoSoValue, US spot Bitcoin ETFs experienced approximately $306.42 million in net outflows on Wednesday.

The withdrawals marked the second consecutive session of negative flows this week, following more than $1 billion in outflows during the previous week.

Persistent ETF withdrawals suggest that investors remain cautious about increasing cryptocurrency exposure amid the recent market downturn.

If the negative flow trend continues, Bitcoin could face additional pressure near important technical support levels. A return to consistent inflows would provide stronger evidence that institutional sentiment is beginning to improve.

Despite the bearish market conditions, on-chain data suggests that Bitcoin may find support near its current trading range.

According to a CryptoQuant report published Tuesday, a significant concentration of long-term holder spending activity occurred between $62,000 and $65,000.

The analysis examined the 30-day sum of long-term holder spending, excluding exchange-related transactions, alongside the prices at which those transactions occurred during 2026.

The highest concentration appeared within the $62,000–$65,000 region. CryptoQuant suggested that the concentration could reflect an important cost-basis area for investors.

Bitcoin remains below major moving averages as bears dominate

Bitcoin's technical outlook remains weak despite its modest recovery from Wednesday's lows. BTC trades around $63,750 on Thursday, significantly below its major daily Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs).

The 50-day EMA stands near $75,238, while the 200-day EMA is positioned around $75,591. Meanwhile, the 100-day EMA sits at approximately $75,730.

These moving averages form a concentrated resistance zone between $75,238 and $75,730. Trading below all three indicators suggests that the broader trend remains bearish across multiple timeframes.

Momentum indicators reinforce this outlook. The daily Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) remains deeply negative, with the MACD line below its signal line and both positioned beneath zero.

This indicates that bearish momentum continues to dominate. Meanwhile, the Relative Strength Index stands near 25, placing Bitcoin in oversold territory.

An RSI reading below 30 generally suggests that selling pressure has become unusually strong relative to recent buying activity.

Bitcoin's immediate outlook depends on whether buyers can defend the support region between $62,000 and $65,000.

The first important downside reference stands near $62,029, followed by the lower boundary of the broader support structure around $61,300.

A sustained breakdown below $61,300 would weaken the near-term technical outlook and increase the risk of a decline toward $60,100.

If selling pressure intensifies further, the $57,803 cycle low could become the next significant downside target.

On the upside, Bitcoin would need to establish stronger buying demand before challenging higher resistance levels.

$69,400 is the initial recovery target if institutional selling begins to ease. A sustained breakout above this level could open the door to $72,700.

Beyond these targets, Bitcoin faces substantial resistance at its major daily moving averages between $75,238 and $75,730.

A decisive recovery above this cluster would provide stronger evidence that the broader bearish trend is beginning to weaken.

Further resistance stands near $85,000, although this level remains distant under current market conditions.

For now, Bitcoin's near-term outlook remains bearish while ETF withdrawals persist and BTC trades below its major moving averages.

data.title: Did Trump discuss Jensen Huang controversy with Xi? Here's what he said
data.description:
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he briefly referred to the controversy surrounding former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang during conversations with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump made these remarks in a Fox News interview aired amid the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

The trade truce between the US and China has been threatened amid the controversy around Nvidia and Huang.

US authorities believe that Alice Huang, who was reportedly involved in a romantic relationship with the former Nvidia boss, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Beijing denies the allegations as US authorities continue to investigate the matter.

What Trump told Jinping

Trump's latest visit to China assumed added significance in the backdrop of the controversy regarding Huang, who had been a prominent opponent of restrictions on chip sales to China.

When asked if Trump had talked to Jinping about Huang, the US President said he touched upon the matter briefly.

He said the pair spoke throughout a dinner the previous evening and that any mention of Huang was limited.

“I might have referred to it just briefly because it’s such a tragedy. It’s a tragedy. He’s such a brilliant man,” Trump said.

He added that he had not heard claims that the Chinese businesswoman linked to Huang was a spy.

Asked if the affair put national security under threat, Trump said, "I haven't heard that."

The remarks came as Nvidia continues to navigate the fallout from Huang’s resignation last week.

Trump has repeatedly backed Huang, even saying he would not mind seeing the co-founder reinstated in his role as CEO.

The exchange between Trump and his Chinese counterpart occurred ahead of a formal bilateral meeting between the two leaders on the sidelines of the APEC gathering, their third encounter this year.

Trump also highlighted what he called strong personal ties with Xi.

US tightens chip exports

Just days before the summit, the US Commerce Department issued new rules aimed at closing loopholes that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced AI chips remotely or through third countries.

The measures impose licensing requirements on shipments to nations including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil, and place additional controls on overseas data centers supplying significant computing power to Chinese entities.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun criticized the move as economic coercion that departs from previous consensus.

​Beijing said that it ​hoped ⁠the US would return to ​the "correct track" ​of ⁠resolving differences through consultation and ⁠cooperation. It also warned of countermeasures if the new rules are enforced.

Nvidia to stop chip sales to China

On its earnings call this week, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is no longer shipping licensed Hopper-generation data-center products, including the H200, to China.

Nvidia recorded $2.4 billion in such sales in the most recent quarter, but Kress stated that future guidance excludes sales in China.

The halt comes despite earlier US approvals for limited licensed shipments.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board has also made clear it does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, even as the former boss himself remains open to returning.

data.title: Anthropic IPO opens the door: 4 tech companies that may go public
data.description:
The upcoming Anthropic IPO has already been highly successful as the company has raised over $80 billion from investors. ANT stock is already up by over 20% in the grey market, and the surge may continue, at least in the near term. As a result, this IPO, which is happening during a bear market for AI companies, may open the door for more listings.

OpenAI may go public after the Anthropic IPO

The most obvious company that will likely go public after Anthropic is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT and the pioneer in the AI space. The company will likely take the cues from Anthropic and launch its IPO.

OpenAI recently raised $11 billion from investors at a $1.25 trillion valuation. It was seeking $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. 

After Anthropic raised over $80 billion, there is a possibility that OpenAI will seek to raise substantial sums of money.

The challenge, however, is that the company’s business is facing substantial headwinds. Its growth has slowed amid the rising competition from companies like Anthropic, Google, and Grok. It is also competing with Chinese companies like Moonshot, Alibaba, and Z.ai.

Anduril plans to go public in 2 years

Palmer Luckey’s Anduril is another company that is watched closely among investors. It has emerged as one of the fastest-growing companies in the world. Also, it has become a disruptor in the defense industry. For example, it is creating a missile interceptor that will cost much less than the Patriot.

Anduril Industries is valued at $124 billion after raising $11.95 billion, making it one of the biggest private companies in the world. Some of its largest investors are Founders Fund, Andressen Horowitz, and Thrive Capital. Anduril has hinted that it will go public in the next two years.

READ MORE: 1789 Capital is raising $3 billion: here are companies in its portfolio

Databricks

Databricks is a top technology company that aims to disrupt Oracle, the biggest database firm in the world. It provides a one platform focusing on data, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI). 

Databricks has raised about $20 billion from investors like Coatue, Blackstone, T.Rowe Price, Sixth Street, and Goldman Sachs. The fundraising has brought its valuation to about $218 billion. 

The company has remained muted on when it will go public. However, estimates are that it will go public either in 2027 or in 2028. 

Stripe

Stripe is another top company to watch. Started in 2011, the company has become one of the biggest private companies in the world with a valuation of $205 billion after raising over $8.7 billion. According to Forbes, Patrick and John Collinson have a net worth of over $9.3 billion each.

Stripe has always been named as one of the top companies that will go public. However, its officials have remained mute on when the company will go public. 

A key challenge for Stripe is that many fintech companies have struggled in public markets. PayPal stock has dropped by over 81% from its all-time high. Other fintech companies like Block, Shift4 Payments, and Fiserv have dropped by over 50%.

Some of the other top companies that may go public are firms like Kalshi, Perplexity AI, Polymarket, Rippling, and Ramp. Nscale, a top British company that provides neocloud services, has already filed to go public. 

Still, a lot could change, especially if Anthropic’s IPO behaves like other recent companies like SpaceX, Circle Internet Group, and Gemini Space Station, there is a likelihood that many of these firms hold back for a while. Also, they will go public if the stock market drops.

data.title: XRP bulls are losing control: could the price crash below $0.90?
data.description:
XRP continues to struggle on Thursday as persistent selling pressure and weakening derivatives activity raise concerns about further losses.

The cryptocurrency is showing signs of bearish positioning in its futures markets, while on-chain indicators suggest that large investors remain cautious.

According to CoinGlass, funding rates for XRP and XLM have turned negative, indicating that traders holding short positions are paying those holding long positions.

Meanwhile, CryptoQuant data shows sell-side dominance across the spot and futures markets of both cryptocurrencies, suggesting that buying demand remains insufficient to reverse the prevailing weakness.

XRP funding rates turn negative as bearish sentiment persists

Derivatives market indicators suggest that traders remain cautious about the near-term outlook for XRP. According to CoinGlass, XRP's funding rate stood at -0.0068% on Thursday. 

Funding rates are periodic payments exchanged between traders holding long and short positions in perpetual futures contracts.

When funding rates are negative, traders holding short positions generally pay those holding long positions. This typically indicates that bearish positioning is more prominent in the perpetual futures market.

Additional derivatives indicators reveal differences in positioning between XRP and Stellar traders. According to CoinGlass, XRP's long-to-short ratio stood at 0.93 on Thursday, approaching its lowest level in more than a month.

A reading below 1 indicates that short positions outnumber long positions under the metric's methodology. This suggests that bearish traders currently have the advantage in XRP's derivatives market.

On-chain and trading activity indicators reinforce the cautious outlook for XRP and Stellar.

According to CryptoQuant, XRP's spot and futures markets are experiencing sell-side dominance, indicating that aggressive selling activity continues to outweigh buying demand.

The broader picture suggests that XRP remains vulnerable to further weakness unless demand improves.

XRP remains below $1 as major moving averages signal weakness

XRP's technical outlook remains bearish as the cryptocurrency struggles to recover above important resistance levels.

The token trades around $0.98 on Thursday, remaining below its major daily Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs).

The 50-day EMA stands near $1.198, while the 100-day EMA is positioned around $1.250. Meanwhile, the 200-day EMA sits at approximately $1.324.

These moving averages form several layers of resistance above the current market price. Trading below all three indicators also means that recovery attempts could encounter selling pressure as prices approach previously important technical levels.

The psychological $1 level represents the first major obstacle. A sustained recovery above this threshold could improve short-term sentiment, but it would not necessarily confirm a broader bullish reversal.

XRP's momentum indicators suggest that the recent decline may be losing some intensity. The daily Relative Strength Index stands near 26, placing the cryptocurrency close to, or just inside, oversold territory.

Meanwhile, the Moving Average Convergence Divergence indicator remains negative, suggesting that bearish momentum continues to dominate.

Nevertheless, the indicator shows signs of moderating downside momentum. This suggests that selling pressure may be easing, potentially allowing XRP to stage a temporary rebound.

XRP faces several important resistance levels as it attempts to recover from its recent decline. The first major barrier stands at the psychological $1 level.

A sustained breakout above this threshold could encourage buyers to target the next horizontal resistance near $1.160. Beyond this level, the 50-day EMA at $1.198 represents another significant obstacle.

A recovery above the 50-day EMA could provide an early indication that short-term bearish momentum is weakening.

However, XRP would still face resistance at the 100-day EMA near $1.250 and the horizontal barrier around $1.300. Further resistance stands at the 200-day EMA near $1.324.

Reclaiming this longer-term moving average would provide stronger evidence of an improving technical structure.

If buying momentum strengthens significantly, additional resistance levels could emerge near $1.540 and $1.900.

For now, XRP's near-term outlook remains bearish while the cryptocurrency trades below $1 and its major daily moving averages.

data.title: Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO eclipses SpaceX, but can its valuation hold?
data.description:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, raising $81.34 billion ahead of its Nasdaq debut and overtaking SpaceX’s original share sale.

The Claude developer expanded its offering to 980 million shares and priced above the indicated $70–$78 range, valuing the company at approximately $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The deal underscores investors’ appetite for artificial intelligence, even as questions grow about whether the industry’s huge computing bills will translate into lasting profits.

Anthropic’s shares are expected to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Investors will now judge whether extraordinary revenue growth can support one of the richest valuations ever assigned to a newly listed company.

Anthropic tops SpaceX’s original IPO, but with a catch

Anthropic increased its offering from 825 million shares to 980 million as demand intensified. The company is selling about 956.35 million shares, with existing shareholders holding the rest.

At $83 apiece, the total sale is worth $81.34 billion. Around $79.38 billion of that represents shares issued by Anthropic, rather than proceeds going to selling investors.

The offering exceeds the $75 billion SpaceX initially raised in June.

However, Elon Musk’s rocket company ultimately collected approximately $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their option to buy additional shares. Anthropic has not yet surpassed that enlarged amount.

A separate $26 billion private placement involving major technology companies could lift Anthropic’s combined equity fundraising above $107 billion, subject to closing. That private transaction is distinct from the IPO itself.

The scale reflects the appeal of owning a direct stake in frontier AI development, an opportunity largely unavailable to ordinary stock-market investors.

Anthropic IPO: Revenue is soaring, but so are computing commitments

Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion in a single month. That is an annualised pace, not revenue already booked over a year.

Actual sales for the first nine months of 2026 reached $33.24 billion, up more than twelvefold from a year earlier. But computing and infrastructure expenses consumed approximately 57% of that revenue.

Anthropic reported an operating loss of about $1.26 billion for the period. Its much larger accounting net loss was heavily affected by non-cash adjustments to financial liabilities, rather than representing equivalent cash spent.

More daunting are roughly $900.9 billion of purchase and lease commitments, principally for computing infrastructure, stretching into 2045. They are multiyear obligations, not bills payable immediately.

Phil Blancato, Osaic’s chief market strategist, told Business Insider that “there’s still room for the business to grow well beyond where it is today”, pointing to AI’s potential across knowledge work.

Anthropic IPO valuation: Can $1.5 trillion valuation survive debut?

At the offering price, Anthropic is valued at roughly 18.5 times its latest annualised revenue run rate. That leaves shareholders dependent on continued expansion and improving margins.

“Great companies, great technology, but are they going to be able to convert this into big profits?” University of Florida IPO researcher Jay Ritter asked in comments to TheStreet.

Competition from OpenAI, Google and cheaper AI models could limit how much Anthropic charges customers, even if adoption keeps growing.

Some professional investors prefer to wait. “We wouldn’t be a buyer at this level,” Strategy Asset Managers chief executive Tom Hulick told Reuters, saying his firm would look for declines after the debut.

Strong initial demand may support the shares, but Anthropic’s first public earnings and any insider selling could test that enthusiasm.

data.title: USD/ZAR just formed a golden cross as South African rand crash continues
data.description:
The USD/ZAR pair made a strong bullish breakout, reaching its highest level since November last year. It jumped to 17.32, up sharply from the August low of 15.90. This rally may continue as the pair has just formed a golden cross pattern and moved above a crucial resistance level. 

South African rand drops as inflation rises

The USD/ZAR exchange rate continued rising after the South African statistics agency published the latest inflation report. This report showed that the headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.7% in October from the previous 0.4%. 

The surge led to an annual increase of 5.2% from the previous month’s 4.5%. The increase was lower than the expected 5.4% and was mostly because of the rising energy prices. Brent and the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) remain at an elevated level during the month.

South Africa’s inflation remained above the South African Reserve Bank’s (SARB) 3% target during the month. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% month on month. This lifted the annual rate to 4.2%, from 4% previously.

The report means that the Federal Reserve may decide to hike interest rates in the final meeting of the year. The bank left interest rates unchanged at 7.25% in its September meeting. Officials hinted that they will need to hike rates again as they predicted that inflation would keep rising in the coming months. 

Another rate hike would bring interest rates to 7.50%, widening the spread with the United States. That move normally creates a good carry trade opportunity, where investors borrow money in low rate countries and invest in high interest rate ones.

The challenge, however, is that the South African economy is slowing. The price of key commodities like gold, platinum, and palladium have dropped, lowering the amount of money coming in to the country. Other metrics like the unemployment rate have worsened, while the Trump administration is removing South Africa from AGOA. 

Federal Reserve rate hike odds are rising

Meanwhile, the USD/ZAR pair has continued rising because of the ongoing US dollar surge. The DXY Index has surged to 103.87, its highest level since April last year. It has soared by over 8.7% from its lowest level this year. Indeed, the dollar has gained against other currencies, including the euro and the British pound. 

The dollar has jumped because of the rising odds that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates in the coming months. Recent macro data showed that the US created over 165k jobs last month. Also, inflation remained stubbornly high during the month. 

As a result, traders on Polymarket, Kalshi, and other prediction marketplaces are betting that the bank will hike interest rates by 0.25% in the December meeting. Indeed, some analysts expect the bank to hike rates by 0.50%.

USD/ZAR technical analysis 

USDZAR chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the USD/ZAR pair has been in a strong upward trend in the past few weeks. After days of consolidating for a few days, the pair made a strong bullish breakout this week, reaching its highest level in a year.

The pair formed an inverted head-and-shoulders pattern, a common bullish reversal pattern in technical analysis. It also formed a golden cross pattern, which happens when the 50-day and 200-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMA) cross each other. 

Therefore, the most likely scenario is where the pair drops to 16.97, its highest point in July this year. It will then bounce back, and potentially hit the pyschological level of 18.

data.title: Trump's Iran strike threat returns, but why aren't oil prices surging?
data.description:
Oil prices struggled to rally on Thursday despite reports that US President Donald Trump was considering fresh strikes against Iran, as rising inventories and recovering Middle Eastern exports kept traders focused on the prospect of excess supply.

Brent crude futures edged up 0.18% to $92.12 a barrel at 02:37 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate slipped 0.11% to $83.17.

The restrained response followed Wednesday's 1.3% fall in Brent. With a possible new military campaign under discussion, the central question is why escalating threats are no longer enough to lift crude prices decisively.

Brent crude oil price: Trump considers further strikes

Axios reported on Thursday that Trump was weighing a joint operation with Israel against Iran, although no decision had been announced.

The White House has sought assessments of possible Iranian retaliation, including attacks on oil and gas facilities in Gulf states.

Gulf leaders are urging restraint, while Israeli officials have raised concerns about suspected Iranian weapons development. Those allegations remain disputed, and Trump indicated on Wednesday that another offensive was not imminent.

Security risks are already tangible, as recent tanker incidents and attacks on regional infrastructure have complicated shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil supplies.

Yet traders appear reluctant to price a prolonged interruption before one materialises and changes the flow of exports.

Vandana Hari, founder of Vanda Insights, described crude as caught between a “persistent geopolitical risk premium” and increasingly bearish expectations of a sizeable surplus, in comments to Reuters on Wednesday.

Oil price forecast: Recovering supply and US stockpiles restrain prices

The International Energy Agency reported that global oil production climbed by 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.4 million, as Gulf exports recovered despite continued attacks.

Observed worldwide inventories rose by 52 million barrels, their first monthly increase since June. The agency expects supply to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, although diesel supplies and onshore stocks remain tight.

US data reinforced the bearish case. Commercial crude inventories increased by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million in the week ended 13 November, according to figures released Wednesday by the Energy Information Administration.

Gasoline stocks rose 5.2 million barrels, while distillate inventories gained 1.6 million. Those builds suggest refiners and distributors have more immediate supply available, weakening the case for a sustained crude rally.

But the recovery remains exposed to sudden setbacks.

Recent attacks near Hormuz “highlight the fragility of this recovery”, Sparta Commodities analyst Abhishek Kumar said in comments reported by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.

His warning underscores that an improving global crude balance does not mean tankers, refineries or fuel markets are secure.

Could another escalation push Brent back towards $100?

An actual interruption to Gulf shipments could change the calculation quickly, particularly if retaliation damages export terminals or closes shipping routes.

Goldman Sachs recently raised its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90, reflecting the risk of renewed supply losses. That estimate is a forecast rather than a guaranteed response to Trump's deliberations.

However, without significant disruption, recovering OPEC+ output and stronger Russian crude exports could continue limiting gains.

ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote on Wednesday that they expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, “limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices”.

Higher US interest-rate expectations and a firm dollar may also restrain consumption and make oil more expensive for overseas buyers.

The next decisive signals will come from Washington's military choices, tanker traffic through Hormuz and subsequent inventory figures.
